item.title: APAC re/insurance markets face shifting risks and growth pressures: Gallagher Re
item.dc:creator: Taylor Mixides
item.category: Artificial intelligence in insurance and reinsurance news

The post APAC re/insurance markets face shifting risks and growth pressures: Gallagher Re appeared first on ReinsuranceNe.ws.
item.content:encoded:
Roshan Perera, CEO of APAC at Gallagher Re, a global reinsurance broker and risk advisory firm, has outlined the key challenges and opportunities facing Asia-Pacific’s insurance and reinsurance markets in the company’s forthcoming APAC Market Watch report 2026, examining slower premium growth, emerging risks and the strategic opportunities created by changing reinsurance market conditions.

According to Perera, insurers across the region have maintained relatively strong profitability and capital positions despite economic uncertainty and geopolitical pressures. Non-life premium growth across the 14 major APAC markets covered by Gallagher Re reached 5% in 2025, although underwriting performance improved in many markets.

Perera identifies portfolio diversification, international expansion and emerging risks as priorities for insurers seeking sustainable growth. Accident and health, cyber, artificial intelligence (AI) and data centre infrastructure are among the areas creating new demand for insurance protection.

He also highlights the potential impact of geopolitical tensions on inflation and claims costs, alongside changing catastrophe exposures linked to climate variability. A potentially strong El Niño event could increase flood risks in Japan, affect agricultural conditions in India and contribute to a higher risk of late-season typhoons. Gallagher Re emphasises the importance of advanced analytics and climate modelling in assessing these exposures.

International expansion is another key trend identified by Perera, with Japanese and South Korean insurers pursuing overseas growth through acquisitions and existing operations. He also points to opportunities in emerging markets as insurers look to diversify beyond their domestic business.

AI presents further opportunities and challenges for the sector. Growing adoption of the technology and investment in semiconductors, data centres and energy infrastructure are creating demand for new insurance solutions. However, Perera highlights potential “silent-AI” exposures, where losses involving AI systems may fall within existing cyber or liability policies without having been specifically anticipated. Gallagher Re has established a Digital Risk Practice to help insurers and reinsurers assess these developing risks.

Reinsurance market conditions are also providing opportunities ahead of the 2027 renewal season. According to Gallagher Re, strong reinsurer balance sheets, abundant capacity and increased competition are creating favourable conditions for buyers. Beyond lower rates, insurers may be able to restructure programmes, adjust retentions and improve capital efficiency.

Despite ongoing uncertainty, Perera notes that underlying insurance performance has improved across much of APAC, with Japan and Taiwan recovering strongly from challenging periods. Specialty insurance, cyber, renewable energy and AI infrastructure are among the areas offering further growth potential.

Gallagher Re works with clients on capital optimisation, reinsurance programme design and expansion into new markets and business lines, combining global expertise with local market knowledge.

Perera’s analysis will feature in Gallagher Re’s APAC Market Watch report 2026, scheduled for publication later this month, which will examine market developments across 14 individual APAC markets.

The post APAC re/insurance markets face shifting risks and growth pressures: Gallagher Re appeared first on ReinsuranceNe.ws.

item.title: Generali advances reinsurance strategy with launch of Syndicate 2031 Red Bridge at Lloyd’s
item.dc:creator: Luke Gallin

For its inaugural Lloyd’s syndicate, Generali has received in-principle approval to commence underwriting operations on the platform in 2027. The large insurer describes […]

The post Generali advances reinsurance strategy with launch of Syndicate 2031 Red Bridge at Lloyd’s appeared first on ReinsuranceNe.ws.
item.content:encoded:
Global insurer Generali has entered the Lloyd’s marketplace with the launch of Syndicate 2031 Red Bridge, which will assume a share of the carrier’s outward reinsurance placements, across multiple lines of business.

For its inaugural Lloyd’s syndicate, Generali has received in-principle approval to commence underwriting operations on the platform in 2027.

The large insurer describes the launch as a “significant step forward” in the Groups’ reinsurance strategy, as the syndicate is designed to optimise its outwards reinsurance programme and risk capital.

Syndicate 2031 Red Bridge will strengthen access to diversified sources of risk capital for Generali, and also reinforce long-term partnerships across the global reinsurance sector, which is line with the firm’s “Lifetime Partner 27: Driving Excellence” strategic plan.

As well as gaining from the financial strength and market reach of Lloyd’s, the world’s oldest insurance and reinsurance marketplace, the new syndicate stands to benefit from the Lloyd’s global licence network, which provides managing agents and syndicates with direct and reinsurance authorisations across more than 200 territories around the world.

Further, via Syndicate 2031 Red Bridge, Generali will bring to Lloyd’s a “distinctive diversification opportunity” in terms of both geographical footprint and type of ceded businesses.

Generali explains that its outward reinsurance book offers significant exposure to risks across continental Europe, which it sees as complementary to Lloyd’s traditional global focus. The portfolio also provides a balanced mix of retail and middle market business access across multiple classes and territories.

Franco Urlini, Group P&C & Reinsurance Officer of Generali, commented: “The launch of Syndicate 2031 Red Bridge marks an important milestone in the evolution of our reinsurance strategy under the “Lifetime Partner 27: Driving Excellence” plan, with the goal to optimise capital at Group level. By leveraging the Lloyd’s global platform, we can develop tailored and innovative risk transfer solutions while accessing new sources of capital to support the growth ambitions of our P&C portfolio. It is an extension of our strategy aimed at maintaining broad and diversified access to reinsurance and alternative capital markets while adding a further tool to the Group’s risk transfer capabilities.”

Dawn Miller, Chief Commercial Officer of Lloyd’s and CEO of Lloyd’s Americas, said: “Our ambition is to attract the leading global underwriters to Lloyd’s, so we are delighted to be welcoming Generali with the launch of Syndicate 2031 Red Bridge. This vehicle will open up deeper connections between insurance, reinsurance and capital markets, underscoring Lloyd’s role as the leading global marketplace for innovative risk transfer solutions.”

item.title: VisionFund, Global Parametrics to develop Amazon Basin parametric cover
item.dc:creator: Saumya Jain
item.description:

The firms said this move aims to address increasingly frequent and severe […]

The post VisionFund, Global Parametrics to develop Amazon Basin parametric cover appeared first on ReinsuranceNe.ws.
item.content:encoded:
VisionFund, the financial inclusion arm of World Vision, working with Global Parametrics and co-financed by the InsuResilience Solutions Fund, will design a two-peril parametric meso-insurance for World Vision offices in Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, and Peru as part of the wider Amazon Basin Initiative.

The firms said this move aims to address increasingly frequent and severe weather events that affect crops and livelihoods, while pushing families deeper into poverty across the Amazon Basin and other climate-vulnerable regions.

The parametric meso-climate insurance solutions will help vulnerable communities respond faster to floods, droughts and other climate shocks, while reducing the financial strain these crises place on families.

VisionFund will leverage its extensive experience to design the solution, starting in the last quarter of 2026, as the Amazon Basin model will also be a template for replication in Southeast Asia and Southern Africa initially.

As it is a parametric model, the solution provides World Vision with pre-arranged funding when satellite-monitored indicators reach predefined thresholds, with automatic payouts to enable the rapid deployment of cash assistance, essential supplies and recovery activities, while reducing its reliance on emergency appeals.

Additionally, a complementary climate decision-making tool translates weather information into practical guidance, enabling World Vision teams and communities to activate contingency plans and take preventive action before a crisis escalates.

Solène Favre, VisionFund Global Director, Inclusive Insurance, commented, “This approach moves disaster and climate response from reactive fundraising towards pre-arranged, predictable protection. By providing a tool that brings institutional risk financing World Vision can implement its pre-planned disaster response activities faster.”

The integrated approach builds on VisionFund’s experience in inclusive insurance, including over eight years of climate meso-insurance and World Vision’s extensive disaster preparedness and response experience in the Amazon Basin region and globally.

item.title: Moody’s RMS says Hurricane Isaias insured losses could hit $4.5bn
item.dc:creator: Beth Musselwhite
item.description:

Hurricane Isaias marks the ninth named storm and the first hurricane of the 2026 North Atlantic hurricane season. On 10 October 2026, […]

The post Moody’s RMS says Hurricane Isaias insured losses could hit $4.5bn appeared first on ReinsuranceNe.ws.
item.content:encoded:
Catastrophe risk modeller Moody’s RMS Event Response has estimated total US private market insured losses from Hurricane Isaias to range from $2.5 billion to $4.5 billion, with a best estimate of $3.5 billion.

Hurricane Isaias marks the ninth named storm and the first hurricane of the 2026 North Atlantic hurricane season.

On 10 October 2026, Isaias made landfall as a Category 2 hurricane near Destin, Florida, with maximum sustained winds of 105 miles per hour (165 kilometres per hour) and a central pressure of 971 hPa.

Hurricane-force winds caused damage near the landfall site on the Florida Panhandle coast and in inland areas extending to the Florida-Alabama border. Coastal areas of the far western Florida Panhandle were affected by a strong storm surge, while rainfall totals of up to 7 inches (180 millimetres) were recorded across the Florida Panhandle and southern and central Alabama.

The system produced tropical storm-force winds across coastal areas of southeastern Louisiana and southern Mississippi, large parts of southern and central Alabama, the Florida Panhandle, and southwestern and central-western Georgia, causing widespread damage from falling trees. It also spawned several tornadoes in the Carolinas.

Moody’s said its recent estimate covers insured losses associated with wind, storm surge and precipitation-induced flooding.

The estimate is predominantly driven by wind damage. Moody’s expects storm surge, precipitation-induced inland flooding and losses to the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) to contribute around $250 million.

The loss estimate reflects property damage and business interruption across residential, commercial, industrial, automobile and watercraft lines of business, and accounts for sources of post-event loss amplification (PLA).

The figure includes wind and storm surge losses in parts of the Gulf Coast and southeastern US, based on analysis of Moody’s RMS Event Response ensemble footprints in Version 25 of Moody’s RMS North Atlantic Hurricane Models. These footprints reconstruct Isaias’s wind and storm surge hazards to account for uncertainties in observed wind speeds and storm surge.

The estimate also includes impacts from precipitation-induced inland flooding in affected regions, using an internal flood footprint reconstruction in Version 1.3 of Moody’s RMS US Inland Flood HD Model.

Other catastrophe modellers have also released insured loss estimates for Hurricane Isaias. Cotality has estimated insured losses from wind and storm surge at between $2 billion and $3 billion.

Karen Clark & Company (KCC) has estimated US privately insured losses from wind and storm surge at $3 billion.

Meanwhile, Verisk’s Catastrophe and Risk Solutions business estimates insured industry losses to onshore property from the hurricane will be between $1 billion and $2 billion.

Gallagher Re has also recently published commentary on Hurricane Isaias, stating that the event is unlikely to influence upcoming 1 January reinsurance renewal discussions.

Jeff Waters, Director – North Atlantic Hurricane Models, Moody’s, commented, “Hurricane Isaias was yet another example of a storm that intensified quickly over the anomalously warm ocean waters in the Gulf, a region that usually sees higher hurricane activity during El Niño years. Thankfully, the storm encountered strong wind shear as it approached landfall, which disrupted its structure and weakened the wind field considerably. As a result, we expect the overall extent and severity of insured losses from this event to be manageable for the market.”

Raj Vojjala, Managing Director – Modeling and Analytics, Moody’s, said, “Many exposures impacted by Hurricane Isaias were also impacted by recent storms like Hurricanes Sally and Zeta in 2020, and Helene in 2024, which led to widespread roof repairs and replacements. We expect these efforts to have improved the risk profile and structural resilience of the region’s building stock to hurricane winds, especially for an event like Isaias. Nevertheless, a high incidence of treefall-driven roof damage in the affected area and potential roof replacements due to Florida’s 25% roof rule, which can require full replacement of certain roofs when repairs exceed a specified threshold, will drive insured losses in this event.”

The post Moody’s RMS says Hurricane Isaias insured losses could hit $4.5bn appeared first on ReinsuranceNe.ws.

item.title: Stand secures $70m Series C Funding to grow resilient home insurance business
item.dc:creator: Taylor Mixides
item.description:
Stand, a property insurance company that helps homes withstand natural disasters, has secured $70 million in Series C funding at a $1 billion valuation. Announced on 15 October 2026, the investment takes the company’s total funding to $130 million. Saga Ventures led the round, which also attracted investment from Lowercarbon, Eclipse, Equal Ventures, Inspired Capital, […]

The post Stand secures $70m Series C Funding to grow resilient home insurance business appeared first on ReinsuranceNe.ws.
item.content:encoded:
Stand, a property insurance company that helps homes withstand natural disasters, has secured $70 million in Series C funding at a $1 billion valuation.

Announced on 15 October 2026, the investment takes the company’s total funding to $130 million.

Saga Ventures led the round, which also attracted investment from Lowercarbon, Eclipse, Equal Ventures, Inspired Capital, Neotribe and Jackson Square Ventures, alongside other investors.

The San Francisco-based company reported that the total value of properties covered by its insurance has reached more than $10 billion, representing a tenfold increase from the $1 billion recorded a year earlier.

Stand aims to expand its portfolio by combining property assessments, practical home improvements and insurance products designed around the level of protection each building offers against natural hazards.

The funding comes as homeowners face growing concerns about the cost and availability of property insurance in areas vulnerable to extreme weather and other natural disasters. Stand argues that conventional insurance models, which often draw heavily on historical loss data, do not always reflect the specific characteristics of individual properties or the improvements that could reduce their exposure to risk.

To address this, Stand has developed a technology-led approach that assesses how homes are likely to respond to different disaster scenarios. Its Stand World Model produces digital representations of properties and simulates their potential performance during events such as wildfires and high winds. The assessments consider factors including building materials, construction methods, surrounding features and local weather conditions.

According to Stand, the model helps identify weaknesses in individual homes and determines which improvements could offer the greatest protection for the cost involved. This allows the company to recommend measures based on the characteristics of each property rather than relying solely on broad risk categories or historical insurance claims.

Stand also assists homeowners with carrying out the recommended work. The company provides guidance throughout the improvement process, connects property owners with its network of trusted partners and verifies that the agreed work has been completed. Its stated objective is to improve a home’s resistance to natural hazards without compromising its existing appearance or character.

After assessing a property’s resilience, Stand offers insurance intended to reflect the reduced risk associated with protective measures. The company says homeowners may qualify for premium reductions of up to 70%. It also aims to offer more consistent pricing and dependable coverage for properties that meet its resilience requirements, helping owners manage the uncertainty associated with insurance renewals.

“Disasters follow the laws of physics, and insurance should too,” commented Dan Preston, Co-founder and Chief Executive of Stand. “If your home is resilient, you should be rewarded with a low premium and never have to worry about losing your coverage. We want to insure every resilient property in the world, and help make every property safe.”

As part of its expansion plans, Stand has appointed two experienced insurance and finance executives to its leadership team. Drew Saad has joined as president of property and casualty, following his most recent role as chief underwriting officer at PURE Insurance. During his time there, he led underwriting operations for the insurer, which specialises in high-net-worth clients.

“The companies that reshape a market for decades are the ones that identify a fundamentally better way to understand risk, and Stand has done that for the homes exposed to natural disasters,” added Saad. “With the science already in place, the opportunity now is to build an insurance operation that matches it and scales it to every market that needs it. That is the work I have spent my career preparing for, and it is why I joined Stand.”

Tony Landi has also joined Stand, taking on the role of chief financial officer. He most recently worked as head of strategic growth at Nephila, a fund manager specialising in catastrophe reinsurance. His previous positions include head of reinsurance and capital management at Openly and head of portfolio management at Everest Re.

In his new position, Landi will be responsible for financial management, reinsurance arrangements, capital markets and the company’s growth strategy. His role includes ensuring Stand has access to the capital needed to support its expanding insurance portfolio and manage its exposure to risk as operations grow.

“What drew me to Stand is the depth of the team, with real experts in physics, underwriting, and product working on the same problem,” noted Landi. “My job is to make sure that as Stand grows, the capital is there to support it, from our investors and our reinsurance partners alike. We’ll do that by building diversified, resilient portfolios and matching risk and returns to capital appetite.”

The $70 million investment will support Stand as it develops its technology and expands its insurance business. With its portfolio of insured properties having grown substantially over the past year, the company is seeking to increase access to insurance for homes that have taken steps to reduce their vulnerability to natural disasters. Its business model centres on linking property-level risk assessments and preventative improvements with insurance pricing, with the aim of making coverage more accessible and predictable for eligible homeowners.

The post Stand secures $70m Series C Funding to grow resilient home insurance business appeared first on ReinsuranceNe.ws.

item.title: Travelers Q3’26 net income rises despite higher cat losses, but 9M cat toll down considerably
item.dc:creator: Kassandra Jimenez-Sanchez
item.description:
Travellers has announced its financial results for the third quarter of 2026, reporting a net income of $1.917 billion, increasing from $1.888 billion in the same period last year, despite a year-on-year rise in catastrophe losses in the period. Core income in the current quarter was $1.947 billion, compared to $1.867 billion in the prior […]

The post Travelers Q3’26 net income rises despite higher cat losses, but 9M cat toll down considerably appeared first on ReinsuranceNe.ws.
item.content:encoded:
Travellers has announced its financial results for the third quarter of 2026, reporting a net income of $1.917 billion, increasing from $1.888 billion in the same period last year, despite a year-on-year rise in catastrophe losses in the period.

Core income in the current quarter was $1.947 billion, compared to $1.867 billion in the prior year quarter. Its increase was primarily due to higher net favourable prior year reserve development – which was favourable for three segments and totaled $234 million pre-tax – and higher net investment income, partially offset by higher catastrophe losses.

Q3 2026’s net income was driven by higher core income, partially offset by net realised investment losses compared to net realised investment gains in the prior year quarter.

Net realized investment losses were $34 million pre-tax ($30 million after-tax), compared to net realized investment gains of $27 million pre-tax ($21 million after-tax) in the prior year quarter.

At 86.8%, the combined ratio improved 0.5 points due to higher net favourable prior year reserve development (1.9 points), partially offset by higher catastrophe losses (1.2 points) and a higher underlying combined ratio (0.2 points). The underlying combined ratio was robust at 84.1%.

Catastrophe losses were up in Q3 2026, Travelers reported an impact of $538 million, which increased from $302 million seen in the same period last year. According to the firm, Q3 2026 cat losses primarily resulted from severe wind and hail storms in multiple states.

Net written premiums of $11.48 billion increased slightly over the prior year quarter. Net written premiums in the prior year quarter included $240 million related to the Canadian operations which the Company divested in the first quarter of 2026.

Excluding the impact of the sale, net written premiums increased 2% over the prior year quarter, Travelers noted.

Year to date 2026, the re/insurer reported a $2.044 billion increase in net income, which reached $5.836 billion. This was driven by higher core income and net realised investment gains compared to net realized investment losses in the first nine months of 2025.

Core income of $5.803 billion increased $1.989 billion, primarily due to lower catastrophe losses, higher net favourable prior year reserve development and higher net investment income.

For the first nine months of 2026, favourable prior year reserve development reached $1.225 billion, an increase compared to the $715 million seen in the same period last year.

Net realised investment gains were $75 million pre-tax ($33 million after-tax), compared to net realised investment losses of $28 million pre-tax ($22 million after-tax) in the prior year period.

Net investment income of $3.176 billion pre-tax ($2.624 billion after-tax) increased 9%, driven by the same factors described above for the third quarter of 2026.

The combined ratio improved 6.9 points to 86.3%, due to lower catastrophe losses (5.4 points) and higher net favorable prior year reserve development (1.6 points), partially offset by a higher underlying combined ratio (0.1 points), which stood at 84.5%.

Natural catastrophe losses in the first nine months of 2026 were significantly down year-on-year, standing at $1.817 billion, from $3.595 billion in the same period in 2025.

Alan Schnitzer, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer, commented: “We are pleased to report excellent third quarter results. It was another in a run of successful quarters, with very strong underwriting performance across all three segments and a record result from our investment portfolio.”

Adding: “Our strong underwriting and investment results through the first nine months of the year reflect the strength of our franchise. We are well positioned to finish the year strong. That momentum, and the advances we are making on our innovation agenda, give us real confidence heading into 2027 and beyond.”

The post Travelers Q3’26 net income rises despite higher cat losses, but 9M cat toll down considerably appeared first on ReinsuranceNe.ws.

item.title: Marsh Re’s Janeke expects Baden-Baden to ‘entrench’ buyer-favourable reinsurance market
item.dc:creator: Kane Wells
item.description:
Marsh Re’s Leon Janeke expects Baden-Baden to “confirm and further entrench” a buyer-favourable reinsurance market ahead of the 1 January renewals, with reinsurers set to take a greater share of large and catastrophe losses as the market rebalances risk. In an interview ahead of the industry event in Germany, Janeke, head of UK Property & […]

The post Marsh Re’s Janeke expects Baden-Baden to ‘entrench’ buyer-favourable reinsurance market appeared first on ReinsuranceNe.ws.
item.content:encoded:
Marsh Re’s Leon Janeke expects Baden-Baden to “confirm and further entrench” a buyer-favourable reinsurance market ahead of the 1 January renewals, with reinsurers set to take a greater share of large and catastrophe losses as the market rebalances risk.

In an interview ahead of the industry event in Germany, Janeke, head of UK Property & Casualty and London Europe at Marsh Re, said reinsurers’ share of insured losses had fallen from around 20% in 2023 to approximately 12%, but he expects it to increase through 2027.

The market remains competitive amid abundant capacity and reinsurers’ search for profitable growth, he said, although it is “not growth at any cost”.

Janeke told Reinsurance News that the market is competitive, but not carefree, adding that reinsurers are willing to partner more broadly with cedents in the current environment.

He added, “There’s a clear focus on price as we head into Baden-Baden and look ahead to the 1 January reinsurance renewals and beyond. Cedents are also looking for value in their placements and seeking to address issues beyond traditional risk transfer. We’re looking more broadly at themes such as volatility and how to control for it.

“So, it’s very much a competitive market, which I would describe as a buyer’s market, but certainly not a carefree one at this point.”

Discussing how the property and casualty markets differ as the renewals approach, Janeke suggested there’s “considerably more optimism” in the property market than in the casualty market currently, from both buyers’ and sellers’ perspectives.

The executive continued, “Starting with property, the reason I use the word optimism is that reinsurers’ share of insured losses has fallen significantly. Marsh has previously highlighted that the reinsurance share stood at around 20% of insured losses in 2023, but has now dropped to approximately 12%, leaving 88% with original cedents.

“That reflects an environment that is currently very profitable for reinsurers, particularly given the lack of major catastrophe losses in the property market. That underlines the optimism we’re seeing.

At the same time, buyers have achieved pricing reductions over the past several years and have been able to bring contract coverage back into line.

“We’re now seeing broad consistency in contract coverage across the market, with relatively few exceptions in terms of the differences between the coverage reinsurers provide to individual cedents. Of course, coverage still varies between cedents at a market level.

“The casualty market is more nuanced, particularly for cedents with exposure to US liability. There’s a much greater degree of caution in this area, owing to familiar concerns around social inflation and reserve uncertainty in long-tail lines of business.

“As a result, the picture is much more mixed in casualty and is far more account-specific. We’re not seeing the same level of optimism in the casualty market at this point.”

Expanding on negotiating leverage ahead of the 1 January renewals, Janeke noted some differences between property and casualty cedents, while acknowledging that many have exposures to both and purchase reinsurance across both segments.

He went on, “From a property perspective, particularly where property is the defining element of a cedent’s reinsurance purchase, there is meaningful negotiating leverage. This is especially true for cedents with clean or very good loss experience over the past several years, which is the case for the vast majority.

“There remains a focus on high-quality exposure data, particularly modelling data. Where that is coupled with a narrative around disciplined underwriting, a well-articulated risk transfer strategy and structures that are well understood at this point in the cycle, cedents have considerable leverage.

“That includes placements without significant structural changes, such as changes to retentions, as well as those where there has been some element of volatility protection in recent years. For those cedents, I think there is tremendous leverage in their reinsurance purchases at this 1 January renewal.

“Looking at multi-class buyers purchasing across property, casualty and specialty lines, we’re seeing the reinsurance market move closer to what buyers have been seeking in terms of broad-based relationships and longer-term partnerships.

“We believe reinsurers have listened to that message and are looking to partner more closely with cedents across their reinsurance purchases than we’ve seen in a very long time.

“There is also a less selective approach, with less cherry-picking of cedents’ exposures. If reinsurers genuinely want to partner with best-in-class cedents, it’s critical that they take a cross-class approach.

Turning to client priorities, we asked Janeke what Marsh Re is hearing from cedents ahead of 1 January. The executive observed that at a high level, clients are looking for better risk transfer value, which, in his view, comes down to two main elements: price and coverage.

Janeke continued, “Clients are definitely looking for further savings in this renewal from their reinsurance panels, but they also want better risk transfer value through enhanced contract coverage.

“As I mentioned earlier, I think we’re back in a market that could broadly be described as concurrent in terms of contract coverage, although there are some areas where that consistency is beginning to fray at the edges. I expect coverage to be broadened in some instances, but I don’t anticipate that being a wholesale theme across the renewal.

“The expectation of further price savings is also firmly established in clients’ messaging and well understood by the market. There’s a clear anticipation of what’s to come on that front.

“We’re also seeing clients look for greater flexibility in programme design as a way of generating better value. That includes multi-year arrangements, and I expect a shift from paid to prepaid reinstatements to become more of a theme this year.

“We’re also seeing considerable flexibility from reinsurers and a willingness to consider value-added elements within certain products, whether frequency or volatility covers.

“We believe there’s a clear appetite to explore how reinsurers can use modelled expected loss to deliver more value through programme design, particularly on the frequency side.”

As the interview drew to a close, the conversation shifted to what Janeke anticipates Baden-Baden will tell us about the key upcoming renewals.

“I expect Baden-Baden to confirm and further entrench the view that this is a buyer-favourable environment. I use the word ‘entrench’ deliberately, because I think that’s exactly what the discussions will do,” the executive said.

He concluded, “We expect some risk rebalancing to take place at the 1 January renewals, by which I mean a shift in the share of large and catastrophe losses borne by reinsurers. As I mentioned earlier, reinsurers currently account for around 12% of insured losses, and we expect that share to increase through 2027.

“I don’t anticipate wholesale changes to retention levels. We are seeing some scope for retentions to come down in parts of Europe, particularly in the French and Nordic markets, but I wouldn’t describe that as a broader European or UK trend at this point. So, in summary, I expect risk rebalancing and a further entrenchment of the buyer-favourable environment.”

The post Marsh Re’s Janeke expects Baden-Baden to ‘entrench’ buyer-favourable reinsurance market appeared first on ReinsuranceNe.ws.

item.title: AI-driven incidents will escalate in frequency once attackers find the right business model: Coalition
item.dc:creator: Kassandra Jimenez-Sanchez
item.category: Artificial intelligence in insurance and reinsurance news
item.description:
Cyber risk can hold flat for years, then jump sharply once attackers find a way to exploit a new technology; artificial intelligence (AI) appears to be heading down a similar path, cyber insurance specialist Coalition believes. The insurance industry collectively has close to a trillion dollars of cyber insurance limits outstanding. Underwriters face two possible […]

The post AI-driven incidents will escalate in frequency once attackers find the right business model: Coalition appeared first on ReinsuranceNe.ws.
item.content:encoded:
Cyber risk can hold flat for years, then jump sharply once attackers find a way to exploit a new technology; artificial intelligence (AI) appears to be heading down a similar path, cyber insurance specialist Coalition believes.

The insurance industry collectively has close to a trillion dollars of cyber insurance limits outstanding. Underwriters face two possible threats from AI: a steady, grinding escalation in the frequency and severity of regular attacks, or a single event that hits many insureds at once.

Industry alarms peaked in September 2026 Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned that an AI swarm could take over “the entire internet” within a year.

The warning was promptly backed by AI executives Sam Altman and Elon Musk, who called for vendors to slow the pace of model development.

The cyber insurance industry has also heard warnings like this before. OpenAI delayed GPT-2’s release in 2019 over malicious-use risk, Turing and Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton resigned from Google in 2023 to warn against existential threats and later flagged sophisticated phishing schemes, and Anthropic withheld Mythos from public release in April 2026 due to concerns about its cyber attack capability.

All of these models were eventually released without destabilizing the cyber insurance market. It’s easy to read that track record as reassurance, but it doesn’t mean that AI will never impact cyber risk.

The cyber threat environment has historically demonstrated initial stability as threat actors test new technology.

A heightened level of risk usually manifests years later, following attackers finding an effective business model to leverage or exploit that innovation. Cybercriminals established the premier online marketplace for trading stolen credit card information in 2001.

Although adoption was initially gradual, this technical advancement ultimately structured an entire illegal ecosystem.

By 2009, law enforcement concluded these forums created a black market for stolen data by allowing “criminals to quickly sell the fruits of their ill-gotten gains to thousands of eager fraudsters.”

Criminals adopting a new technology made data breaches profitable. Businesses holding sensitive data experienced a dramatic increase in data breach risk, but only years after criminals started using online forums.

In the 2010s, ransomware actors began demanding cryptocurrency payments. Initially targeting individual machines for minor sums, they found little success because victims preferred replacing hardware over paying in unknown digital currencies.

The strategy became profitable only after attackers transitioned to compromising full networks.

Unable to bypass the threat, victims learned to pay in cryptocurrency, allowing attackers to collect million-dollar ransoms, untraceable by law enforcement Though this shifted the risk landscape slowly, by 2020, after the cryptocurrency-back ransom model gained traction, ransomware incidents surged over 1,000% from 2017’s claims, with a maximum losses soaring from $500,000 to $20 million.

By 2025, ransomware represented 75% of all claims paid by the cyber insurance industry.

Coalition sees the same pattern taking shape with AI today, moving fastest where the underlying attack was already easy to automate, and slower where more manual steps stand in the way.

While widespread disruption has not yet crippled balance sheets, the incubation phase is well underway, Coalition stated.

item.content:encoded:
Lloyd’s has granted in-principle approval for the establishment of Credeq Syndicate 1998, marking a significant step in Credeq’s global growth strategy.

Headquartered in London, Credeq is a global specialist credit risk insurance provider, with expertise spanning Guarantees & Surety, Trade Credit, Credit Risk Insurance and AI Risk. It operates across the UK, Europe, Africa, Australia and New Zealand.

Credeq Syndicate 1998 is expected to begin underwriting on 1 January 2027, subject to completion of the remaining implementation requirements and receipt of final Permission to Underwrite.

The syndicate’s underwriting plan will focus on credit risk insurance, as well as surety reinsurance and speciality European trade credit. It will provide additional, strategically aligned capacity to support Credeq’s existing credit risk business and create opportunities for further growth, complementing its existing capacity partnerships.

Credeq will act as coverholder for the syndicate, bringing its underwriting expertise and global origination network to the Lloyd’s market. Asta Managing Agency has been appointed as managing agent for Credeq Syndicate 1998, while Marsh Capital & Advisory advised on the syndicate’s formation.

Through the combination of Credeq’s specialist credit underwriting expertise with Lloyd’s global reach and financial security framework, it will provide Credeq greater flexibility to support clients and pursue opportunities across its international markets.

Martin McConnell, co-CEO and head of credit risk insurance at Credeq said, “Establishing our own specialist underwriting capacity within Lloyd’s is a major milestone for Credeq. It brings together our deep credit risk expertise and global origination capability with the unmatched financial strength and global reach of the world’s leading insurance marketplace.

“The syndicate gives us additional, strategically aligned capacity to support our clients and underwrite complex credit risks across our markets, while complementing the strong capacity partnerships we already have in place.

“It is an important next step in building Credeq’s global specialist credit business.”

Lorraine Harfitt, Chief Executive Officer of Asta added, “We are delighted to partner with Credeq as the business takes this important step towards entering the Lloyd’s market. Receiving in-principle approval from Lloyd’s for this unique proposition is testament to the strength of the partnership we have already built together, and we are excited to support the Credeq team as they launch and establishes their presence in the market.”

item.content:encoded:
Nepal and the World Bank (International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, IBRD) have signed a mandate agreement to explore the development of a catastrophe bond for quicker access to funds in case of a major earthquake.

The agreement between the two parties marks the beginning of a collaboration to assess how capital markets can support Nepal’s broader disaster risk management strategy.

The initiative is part of the World Bank Group’s established catastrophe bond program, which allows countries to access international capital markets to transfer disaster risk and secure financial protection against natural hazards.

As reported in July on our sister site, Artemis, it is understood that this proposed cat bond is going to be parametric in nature, meaning it would be designed to pay out based on pre-defined physical earthquake parameters, and targets USD 80-190 million of fully-collateralised disaster risk financing from the capital markets for the South Asian country.

These parameters could include magnitude and the severity of ground shaking, rather than actual assessments of financial and economic losses, it is anticipated.

Nepal is one of the world’s most disaster-prone countries and faces significant seismic exposure and earthquakes. The country said that it is working to better prepare for, withstand, and recover from future natural disasters through a combination of risk reduction, preparedness, and financial protection measures.

For context, on 26 August 2026, a Himalayan glacier and rock collapse near the Nepal-China border triggered flash flooding along an approximately 70-kilometre stretch of the Trishuli River, devastating communities across the Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts, resulting in significant humanitarian and economic losses.

According to analysts at AM Best, international reinsurers are expected to absorb a significant share of the event’s overall modest insured losses as the country’s non-life insurance market relies heavily on reinsurance capacity to underwrite catastrophe risks.

Under the agreement, the World Bank Group Treasury will work with the Government of Nepal and market participants to assess the feasibility and potential structure of the catastrophe bond.

If this project goes ahead, it would be the first catastrophe bond to cover risks in Nepal and a rare cat bond covering South Asian exposures.
